strengths: The paper applies data attribution (gradient-similarity influence estimation) to a novel and practically relevant problem—tracing unsafe model behaviors back to training data—rather than relying purely on content-level moderation classifiers.

The observation that naively attributing long-form unsafe outputs yields noisy attribution (benign tokens dilute the unsafe-token signal) is well motivated and empirically supported (Appendix B.1, Tables 8–10, Figure 1), and the proposed remedy of using a small externally verified unsafe subset as the attribution target yields large gains (Table 9: AUPRC 4.70% → 52.0% on ToxicChat).
Evaluation goes beyond detection metrics: retraining after DABUF filtering produces measurably safer models (Table 4, Table 7), which is the metric that ultimately matters for the claimed use case.
Two different unsafe-data regimes are studied (adversarial jailbreak injections and inherent gender bias), with an appropriate ablation showing robustness to validation/target set size (Figure 2).

The limitations section is honest and substantive, including discussion of adversarial attacks on attribution (Wang et al., 2024d), and key experimental details (LoRA, checkpoints, hardware, hyperparameters) are provided in Appendix C.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is a central concern: DABUF's jailbreak pipeline relies on Llama-Guard-3-8B screening plus human annotation of the candidate set to construct the attribution target, while the baselines (Llama-Guard, Wildguard, GradSafe, OpenAI API) receive no such human verification. This makes it unclear how much of the gain comes from data attribution versus the extra human-labeled supervision, and it undercuts the paper's framing that the method 'eliminates the need for data curation' and operates 'without predefined taxonomies'—in practice the method is a hybrid that still depends on a moderation classifier and taxonomy for candidate generation.

The experimental setups are artificial and largely within-distribution: the injected unsafe data and the target set are drawn from the same dataset (ToxicChat/XSTest splits), so attribution largely reduces to retrieving samples from a known distribution; the paper's own Limitations section concedes that heterogeneous injections are untested. The gender-bias injection (flipping physician→nurse labels on female biographies) is a very narrow, synthetic corruption, and the only baseline is a generic embedding similarity method (Ada3), which is a weak comparison.

Evaluation sets are very small: |Dtest| = 30 and 20 unsafe prompts for ASR, |Dunsafe| = 97 and 65 for detection. Differences such as 86.7% vs. 90.0% ASR in Table 4 are a few test examples and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for the main tables.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: on XSTest-Response, Wildguard clearly outperforms DABUF in AUPRC (85.9 vs. 74.1) and F1 (71.1 vs. 68.7); DABUF only wins on ToxicChat and in the retraining/ASR experiments. The explanation that XSTest 'aligns with in-distribution training data' for the classifiers highlights that DABUF's advantage is scenario-dependent.

The method requires the contaminated model to have already been fine-tuned and gradient features computed over the full training set (with LoRA/random projection), followed by retraining after filtering; the computational cost relative to simply running a moderation classifier over the data is never quantified, weakening the efficiency argument against fine-tuned classifiers.

Presentation issues remain, including grammatical errors ('we first an LLM-based classifier to screen'), confusing results such as the high baseline ASR when training on Dbenign only (66.7–83.3% in Table 1), and no mention of code release, which limits reproducibility.

strengths: The problem of identifying unsafe training data by tracing unsafe model outputs back to training samples via data attribution is a well-motivated and relatively underexplored angle, distinct from purely content-based moderation classifiers.

The paper provides useful analysis of why naive whole-response attribution is noisy (Appendix B.1, Table 8, Table 9), with a clear ablation showing that unsafe tokens such as 'poison' and 'commit' are far more informative attribution targets than common words, and that attribution on model responses performs dramatically worse (AUPRC 4.7% vs. 52.0%).

The downstream evaluation (retraining after filtering and measuring ASR / TPR Gender Gap) is a sensible and more meaningful metric than detection scores alone, and the validation-set-size ablation (Figure 2) shows the method degrades gracefully to ~20 validation samples.

Both jailbreak injection and gender bias scenarios are covered, spanning two model families (Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B), and the limitations section is candid, including a discussion of adversarial attacks on data attribution (Wang et al., 2024d).
weaknesses: The central advantage claimed over moderation classifiers is substantially undermined by the method itself: in the main (jailbreaking) setting, DABUF first requires Llama-Guard-3-8B to screen the full training set and then requires human annotation of the candidate set to build the attribution target. The method is therefore a hybrid that still depends on a predefined-taxonomy classifier plus costly human labeling, contradicting the framing of 'flexible identification without predefined taxonomies' and 'eliminating the need for data curation'.

The core hypothesis—unsafe training data exerts greater influence on unsafe outputs—is close to assumed rather than established. Gradient similarity may simply capture lexical overlap between injected samples and the target set; the paper does not control for or analyze whether attribution is detecting causal influence versus surface similarity, which is the crux of the contribution.

The evaluation scale is very small and statistically fragile: test sets contain only 30 and 20 unsafe prompts (ToxicChat, XSTest-Response), injection ratios below 0.025%, and no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the headline results. Several key deltas (e.g., ASR 86.7% vs. 90.0%, i.e., a single test example) are within noise.

Results are inconsistent with the SOTA claims: Wildguard outperforms DABUF on XSTest-Response detection (85.9 vs. 74.1 AUPRC), and the explanation ('in-distribution training data') is post-hoc and untested. Notably, Table 1 shows ASR of 66.7–83.3% even when training only on the benign dataset, raising questions about whether the threat model and the safety gains in Table 4 are well-characterized.

The gender bias experiment is artificially constructed as a label-corruption poison (150 female physician biographies relabeled 'nurse'), which is closer to a mislabeled-data detection task than genuine gender-bias mitigation, and the only baseline is a single embedding similarity method (Ada3) with no attempt to adapt the moderation classifiers that were used in the other experiment; the headline '44.1% improvement' rests on this weak comparison.

Practicality concerns are not addressed: the method requires fine-tuning and per-dataset attribution on models up to 9B with LoRA gradients, but no compute/runtime comparison against classifiers is provided, despite motivating the paper partly by the cost of fine-tuned moderation models.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, attribution hyperparameters (projection details, optimizer-aware gradient choices) are only partially specified, and the human annotation protocol for building D_identified (inter-annotator agreement, guidelines) is absent.

Presentation has noticeable flaws, e.g., a grammatically broken sentence ('we first an LLM-based classifier (Llama-3-Guard-8B...) to screen'), and the notation for precision/recall uses a held-out 'validation set' interchangeably with D_test in ways that require careful reader reconstruction.

strengths: Novel and sensible framing: recasting unsafe training data detection as a data attribution problem, tracing unsafe model behaviors back to influential training points rather than relying purely on content-moderation classifiers.

The paper clearly identifies and motivates a real technical failure mode — dilution of unsafe-token gradients by benign tokens in long-form outputs — and supports it with empirical analysis (Appendix B.1, Tables 8-10 showing token-level AUPRC differences and Response vs. DABUF comparisons).

Evaluation goes beyond detection metrics to downstream utility: retraining on DABUF-filtered data yields lower Attack Success Rate (Table 4) and reduced TPR Gender Gap (Table 7), which is the more meaningful claim for a data-filtering method.

Two distinct and complementary settings (adversarial jailbreak injection with long noisy outputs; gender bias with concise outputs) demonstrate the flexibility of the approach beyond predefined safety taxonomies.

Reasonable ablations: varying attribution-target token sets (Figure 1) and validation-set size (Figure 2) with repeated sampling and error bars; honest limitations section discussing homogeneous injections, missing taxonomy, and adversarial manipulation of influence scores.
Practical scalability choices (gradient similarity with random projection to d=8192, LoRA) make attribution feasible for ~8-9B models where full influence functions would not be.
weaknesses: The pipeline depends on human annotation of a classifier-screened candidate set (Didentified) for the jailbreak experiments. This contradicts the framing of DABUF as a flexible, human-effort-free alternative to moderation classifiers, and the baseline comparisons do not account for this extra cost; a pipeline of Llama-Guard + human verification + attribution is materially different from a pure classifier.

Statistical evidence is thin. Test sets for ASR are extremely small (|Dtest| = 30 and 20), so differences such as 90.0% vs. 86.7% (one sample) in Table 4 are not reliable, and no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the headline detection and retraining results. Baseline ASR for the 'benign-only' model is itself high (66.7% for Llama-3-8B on ToxicChat), further muddying interpretation.

The 'outperforms SOTA' claim is overstated. On XSTest-Response, Wildguard (85.9 AUPRC, 71.1 F1) and Llama-Guard (82.5, 68.7) both beat DABUF (74.1, 68.7); DABUF only clearly wins on ToxicChat AUPRC. The abstract's 'up to 7.5%' should be qualified accordingly.

The gender-bias comparison is weak: the only baseline is an off-the-shelf embedding model (Ada3) with near-random AUPRC (0.089), and the injected bias is constructed by a simple label corruption (physician→nurse) that is well aligned with the self-generated attribution targets, raising circularity concerns. The '44.1% improvement' is against this weak baseline only.

All AUPRC values are low in absolute terms (best 52-53%), indicating the task remains largely unsolved and that gradient-similarity attribution provides only modest absolute detection quality; the practical value of the retrieved sets beyond top-100 is unclear.

Both experiments use synthetic injection setups where unsafe data comes from the same or closely related distribution as the target set, which the limitations section acknowledges; generalization to heterogeneous or organic contamination is not demonstrated.

Novelty is primarily in the application and the targeted-attribution heuristic; the core machinery (TracIn-style gradient similarity, following Xia et al. 2024) and the moderation-classifier screening step are borrowed, so the methodological contribution is incremental.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, human annotation protocol details (annotator agreement, criteria for verifying Dcand) are not reported, and single-seed training/retraining is implied throughout. Minor writing issues (e.g., 'we first an LLM-based classifier' in Sec. 3.1) suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The paper is well motivated: it identifies a concrete, plausible limitation of representation-based data attribution for unsafe data detection (averaged representations are dominated by neutral content), and grounds the proposed fix in signal detection theory via the discriminability index d'.

The proposed DRA method is simple, principled, and cheap: centering + whitening (Mahalanobis correlation) plus eigenvector dimension selection by a leave-target-out discriminability score. Appendix E ablations confirm both components contribute and are complementary, and Appendix D provides empirical support that d' is a reasonable proxy for AUPRC.

Evaluation goes beyond detection metrics: the paper shows end-to-end utility by retraining models on filtered data and reporting ASR (jailbreak) and TPR Gender Gap (bias), demonstrating that DRA-filtered data yields meaningfully safer models (e.g., Gemma ASR 3.0% vs 77.0% for GradSim on XSTest).

The experimental setup follows a standardized benchmark (DATE-LM) with established datasets (UltraChat, ToxicChat, XSTest-Response, Bias in Bios), enabling direct comparison to moderation-classifier baselines (Llama-Guard, Wildguard, OpenAI Moderation API) across two model families.

The analysis of target-set size (Appendix C.2) is practically useful, showing DRA remains effective with as few as 3 target samples and scales better than raw GradSim, and the t-SNE visualizations give intuitive evidence that whitening/selection separates unsafe from benign gradients.

Limitations and potential risks are discussed honestly, including heterogeneous injection settings, lack of fine-grained taxonomy, and susceptibility to adversarial manipulation of attribution scores.
weaknesses: The core technique is a fairly incremental combination of standard tools (covariance whitening, PCA, eigen-dimension selection); the main novelty is the LTO d' selection criterion, which is heuristic. The claimed circularity concern is real: d'_LTO selects dimensions by detecting the target set Q itself within D_train ∪ Q, so dimension selection directly optimizes for similarity-to-Q, which may overfit the target set and inflate gains when D_target and D_unsafe share distributional quirks. A held-out validation of selected dimensions would strengthen the claims.

Statistical rigor of the retraining experiments is limited: ASR results rely on small test sets with 10 inference runs but no confidence intervals, no multiple retraining seeds, and some anomalies are left unexplained (e.g., Table 3: GradSim filtering on Llama/ToxicChat yields ASR 34.7%, worse than no filtering at 33.3%; RepSim-DRA on Gemma yields 30.7%, worse than RepSim 29.0%). Differences such as 26.0% vs 27.3% may be within noise.

The unsafe data is synthetically injected and relatively homogeneous (corrupted-label bios, single-distribution jailbreak sets), as the authors acknowledge; evidence for generalization to organic, heterogeneous unsafe data in the wild is missing.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: two models (8-9B), LoRA-based fine-tuning only, and the bias evaluation is restricted to a single physician/nurse TPR-gap construct; sensitivity of results to the fixed r=30 dimensions and reduced candidate set m' is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned, key hyperparameters (r, m', K for filtering) lack justification or sensitivity analysis, and details such as which layer's hidden states are used for RepSim are not fully specified.

The d'-AUPRC monotonicity claim is only 'under certain technical assumptions' and is validated empirically in a limited setting (single-dimension scores, Appendix D); the theoretical grounding is thus looser than the framing suggests.

The motivation about 'critical tokens vs neutral tokens' is not directly tested (e.g., no token-level analysis demonstrating that neutral tokens cause the noise); the connection between the narrative and the whitening mechanism is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: The paper is framed on a standardized, public benchmark (DATE-LM) with well-defined injection protocols (ToxicChat, XSTest-Response, Bias-in-Bios), making the evaluation directly comparable to prior baselines rather than a bespoke setup.

The core idea is clearly articulated and theoretically motivated: representations are 'noisy' for unsafe-data detection, so center/whiten (a Mahalanobis-style score, Lemma 3.1) and then select eigen-dimensions via a leave-target-out discriminability index. The two components are cleanly separated and ablated (Table 7), showing each contributes.

Evaluation goes beyond detection AUPRC to a downstream retraining experiment (ASR, TPR Gender Gap), which is the more meaningful end metric for filtering, and includes moderation-classifier baselines (Llama-Guard, Wildguard, OpenAI API).

The target-set-size analysis (Fig. 3) is practically relevant, showing DRA outperforms Wildguard with as few as 3 target samples, and the Limitations section honestly discusses homogeneous injection, taxonomy limits, and adversarial risks to attribution.
The method is lightweight relative to fine-tuned moderation classifiers, requiring no additional labeled safety data.
weaknesses: A central methodological concern is circularity: the leave-target-out dimension selection uses the target set Q as a surrogate for the unknown unsafe training distribution U, optimizing dimensions that best separate Q from X. This directly bakes in the very hypothesis being evaluated (that unsafe training data resemble unsafe model outputs). The selection is performed on the same data used for final AUPRC evaluation, with no held-out split or cross-validation of the dimension selection, so reported gains may be partly overfitting to the target set. The r=30 dimension budget is reported as fixed 'across experiments' without justification of how it was chosen.

The headline '+63.3% AUPRC' is a relative gain over GradSim on XSTest-Response where GradSim scores 1.7% — a near-degenerate baseline — making the improvement number misleading; absolute gains (e.g., 1.7→81.5) should be the primary reporting, and several Deltas are driven by extremely weak baselines (e.g., RepSim 0.9% AUPRC on gender bias).

Retraining evidence is mixed and under-powered: several filtered models are *less* safe than the D_train baseline (GradSim 34.7% vs 33.3% ASR; RepSim-DRA 30.7% vs 28.0% on Gemma), ASR values move in small increments (2–3 percentage points, plausibly single test examples given the small test splits) with no confidence intervals or significance testing, and only a single seed/last checkpoint is used.

Novelty is modest: the plug-in score is a standard Mahalanobis-distance detector, and eigen-dimension selection is a common whitening/PCA-based trick. The theoretical content (Lemma 3.1, d' as surrogate) is textbook signal detection theory; the claimed monotonicity of d' with AUPRC holds only under Gaussian assumptions that are unlikely to hold for LLM representations, and the empirical validation (Fig. 4) covers only single-dimension scores.

The comparison framing is somewhat asymmetric: DRA requires white-box access to the fine-tuned model, gradients/hidden states, and a target set of unsafe outputs, while moderation classifiers are model-agnostic and usable pre-deployment; the paper acknowledges this but the abstract's 'outperforming SOTA' claim glosses over these stronger assumptions.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or artifact release is mentioned, key details (m', r selection, K for filtering, how the target set is constructed across the 10 runs) are scattered or unspecified, and the gender-bias scenario uses an artificial, small-scale corruption (150 of 10,000 samples, physician→nurse relabeling) whose realism is questionable.

Presentation issues: the Delta column semantics shift between tables (relative AUPRC improvement vs. absolute ASR decrease), RepSim vs. 'Repsim' naming inconsistency, and the LTO surrogate approximation for U is asserted rather than empirically validated against ground-truth unsafe data.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper casts unsafe training data detection in signal detection theory terms and derives a principled objective (maximizing discriminability d'), which gives theoretical grounding to an otherwise heuristic area.

The proposed DRA method is simple, computationally lightweight (centering, whitening, and eigen-dimension selection), and does not require training a moderation classifier, making it attractive for flexible adaptation beyond predefined taxonomies.

Substantial empirical gains over the vanilla attribution baselines it builds on (e.g., +63.3% AUPRC for GradSim-DRA on ToxicChat), with ablations (Table 7) showing that both the denoising and dimension-selection components contribute, and a target-set-size study (Figure 3) demonstrating practicality with as few as 3 target samples.

Evaluation covers two distinct unsafe-data scenarios (jailbreak injection and implicit gender bias) and two backbone models, and demonstrates downstream benefit via retraining with reduced ASR and TPR Gender Gap, not just detection metrics.

The limitations section is honest and substantive, discussing homogeneous injection assumptions, lack of fine-grained taxonomy, and potential adversarial manipulation of influence scores (Wang et al., 2024b).
The empirical validation that d' correlates monotonically with AUPRC (Figure 4, Appendix D) supports using d' as the selection objective.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core ingredients (Mahalanobis whitening, covariance-based detection, greedy feature selection) are standard; Lemma 3.1 is a classical signal detection result, and the contribution is essentially a well-executed application of known techniques to a new setting. The paper would benefit from more precise positioning of what is new beyond GradSim/RepSim.

Concerns about circularity/realism in the evaluation setup: the target set D_target is defined as the union of unsafe model outputs collected across evaluation runs, and injected unsafe data is homogeneous and synthetic (corrupted labels, ToxiChat injections into UltraChat). This departs from the heterogeneous, realistic unsafe data the paper motivates, and the dependence on already-identified unsafe model outputs weakens the claimed advantage over moderation classifiers in deployment.

Statistical rigor of the retraining results is insufficient: ASR values are reported without confidence intervals or variance across the 10 runs, test sets appear small (ASR granularity of 3% on XSTest), and some filtered models score worse than the unfiltered baseline (e.g., GradSim on ToxicChat 34.7% vs. D_train 33.3%), making the claimed up-to-39.9% ASR reduction hard to assess. No significance testing is provided.

Some baseline results appear anomalously low (e.g., GradSim AUPRC of 1.7% for Llama-3-8B on XSTest-Response, well below Gemma's 50.2%), raising questions about baseline configuration or tuning, and improvements are partly measured against weak baselines; Llama-Guard-3-8B already achieves 91.6/93.0 on XSTest, so the 'outperforms SOTA moderation classifiers' claim holds only in some settings.

Key hyperparameters and assumptions are under-explored: the fixed dimension size r=30 is used across all experiments without sensitivity analysis, the choice of m' top eigenvectors is not justified, and the critical assumption that the target mean mu_Q approximates the unknown unsafe mean mu_U is not directly validated.

The method still requires a small set of labeled unsafe target examples, and the covariance/dimension selection uses representations from the contaminated training set X, both of which complicate the framing of DRA as requiring 'no additional labeled data' relative to classifiers.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, evaluation protocols span multiple appendix sections, and relevant recent baselines (e.g., LARF, which is cited and closely related) are discussed but not empirically compared.

Presentation issues: inconsistent capitalization and naming (Repsim/RepSim, 'Grad-Sim-Dr-Unsafe' in Figure 3 vs. GradSim-DRA elsewhere), duplicate citations (De-Arteaga et al. 2019a/b), and typos ('emphirical', 'detect' vs 'detects').
